read.headline: Zero new listings, five price cuts and eight departures: inventory fell from 74 to 66 without a single home arriving to replace what left.
points: Inventory. 66 homes are active, down from 74 — the largest single-refresh drop this tracker has recorded, and the first with no new listings at all. 18 sit inside the four 9/10 catchments (Newport Heights 11, Somerset 6, Audubon 1, Woodridge 0) and 48 across the two ZIP sweeps. 24 listings are under $1.5M, but only 5 of those are in a strong catchment and all five are Newport Heights homes between $1,280,000 and $1,400,000 — the same five as Saturday, unchanged in price. The median strong-catchment asking price is $1,772,500, well above the $1.5M line.

Momentum. Since the last refresh: no new listings, 5 price cuts worth $347,000, 5 homes under contract and 3 off the market — two closed sales and one genuine withdrawal. That is 8 out and 0 in over 3 days. Cuts are now carried by 30 of the 66 active listings, $1,958,089 in total. Both ZIP medians moved to their June vintage and both moved down: 98008 to $1,379,688 at -10.1% YoY, 98052 to $1,324,701 at -3.3% YoY.

What pending actually says. Five contracts against three departures is not evidence of buyers absorbing inventory, and the raw pending count of 26 is not a demand gauge. Pending is a stock draining on a 30-45 day escrow clock, not a weekly flow, so it accumulates whatever has not yet closed. The measure that means something is how long a home sat before an offer arrived: across the 26 homes now under contract the median was 42 cumulative days, the middle half ran 17 to 81 days, and only 8 of 26 — 31% — found a buyer inside a month.

And 42 days is flattering. It is computed only from homes that found buyers. The ones still listed have not yet contributed their larger numbers, so the true wait is longer than the completed contracts suggest. The 90-day cohort is the cleaner cut: 19 tracked homes have passed three months on market, 15 of them are still active and 4 reached contract — and that 4 is a lower bound, because a home loses its cumulative-days figure once it closes. 6 of the 26 pendings had cut price before finding a buyer. What none of this shows is deals falling apart: the carried-over pendings are 3 to 30 days into escrow, a median of 17, which is an ordinary closing timeline rather than a warning sign.

Time on market. Median cumulative days across the 66 active listings is 48, essentially flat against 51 on Saturday — but flat here is the arithmetic of losing eight homes, not of anything selling faster. 15 listings have been on more than 90 days, and the tail runs to 313 at 16707 NE 124th St, with 7337 151st Ave NE at 164 and 13307 NE 77th St at 151 behind it. The withdrawal of 5733 155th Ave NE at 235 days is what a listing that never finds its price eventually does.

Financing. The 30-yr fixed is 6.69% (Freddie Mac, Aug 6), unchanged from the last refresh. At the default $1.5M / 20% down case that is $7,735/mo of principal and interest and $10,198/mo all-in with tax and insurance, against a 4BD rent comp of $4,893/mo stamped 2026-08 — an ownership premium of roughly $5,300 a month before any equity credit, and about $4,200 after crediting the $1,078/mo of first-year principal. The rent comp is 11 days old and is not due for re-deriving until September.

Entry price. The cheapest active home is $1,099,888 (24 158th Pl SE, Bellevue 98008); the cheapest in a 9/10 catchment is $1,280,000 (4333 123rd Ave SE, Newport Heights), unchanged for several refreshes. Nothing under $1.5M arrived this refresh and nothing under $1.5M left, so the affordable end of the board is exactly where it was — the churn happened above it.

Implication. At the default $1.5M / 20% down / 6.69% / 7-year case the calculator still leans rent, by about $169,700, with buying pulling ahead around year 14. That breakeven is highly sensitive to the appreciation assumption: 3%/yr puts it at roughly year 14, 1%/yr at roughly year 27, and at 0% renting stays cheaper for the full 30 years. Both ZIP medians are currently negative year-over-year — -10.1% and -3.3% — so the default 3% is an assumption, not an observation. What this refresh adds is supply-side: eight homes left and none arrived, which thins the board without anything in the pricing data suggesting urgency.

read.headline: 74 active listings, a median 51 days on market, and — once you measure it properly — a market where the typical home waits 44 days for an offer and four out of five listings past 90 days are still sitting.
points: Inventory. 74 homes are active, 20 of them inside the four 9/10 catchments and 54 across the two ZIP sweeps. The strong-school split is lopsided: Newport Heights 11, Somerset 8, Audubon 1, Woodridge 0 — the Woodridge listing left this refresh and nothing replaced it. 27 listings sit under $1.5M, but only 5 of those are in a strong catchment, and all five are Newport Heights homes between $1,280,000 and $1,400,000.

Momentum. Since the last refresh: 11 new listings, 11 price cuts worth $815,383, 6 homes under contract and 2 off the market — one of which closed and only one of which was a true withdrawal. Cuts cluster in Bellevue 98008 and Redmond 98052, which is also where the medians are softest: $1,469,064 and −5.2% YoY in 98008, $1,302,113 and −3.9% YoY in 98052, both still at the May 2026 vintage.

What pending actually says. Six contracts against two departures invites the reading that buyers are absorbing inventory. The days-on-market data does not support it, and the earlier version of this read got it wrong. Pending is a stock draining on a 30-45 day escrow clock, not a weekly flow, so counting contracts against departures compares two quantities moving on different timescales. The honest demand measure is how long a home sat before an offer arrived: median 44 days, middle half from 18 to 84, and only 29% under contract within a month.

And that 44 days is flattering. It is computed only from homes that found buyers; the ones still listed — median 51 days and climbing, out to 313 — have not yet had their number counted, so the true wait is longer than the completed sales suggest. The cleanest available cut is the 90-day cohort: of 21 tracked homes that passed three months on market, 17 are still active and 4 reached contract, so past that mark a listing is about four times likelier to be sitting than in escrow. Four of the 21 pendings cut first, $393,000 between them — 1759 173rd Ave NE took $198,000 off before going pending at 68 days; 16813 NE 33rd St, reference home A, took $78,000 off and went pending at 108. What this is not is evidence of collapsing deals: the 15 carried-over pendings are a median 14 days into escrow, which is simply normal.

Financing. The 30-yr fixed printed 6.69% on Aug 6, up 3 basis points from 6.66% the week before. At that rate a $1,500,000 home with 20% down costs $10,198/mo to hold — $7,735 principal and interest, $1,063 tax, $1,400 insurance — against a rent comp of $4,893/mo, re-derived this refresh from 70 active 4BD rentals. Over seven years the model puts buying at $525,893 net and renting at $355,498, a $170,395 gap in renting's favor.

Entry price. The cheapest strong-school listing is 4333 123rd Ave SE at $1,280,000 in Newport Heights, and at 13 days on market it has not yet had time to prove anything: $8,724/mo to own at 20% down, a seven-year gap of $79,234, breakeven around year 11. Reference home C at $1,498,000 after its $50,900 cut runs $10,184/mo and breaks even at year 14 — and is zoned to a 5/10 elementary, so it buys square footage rather than school access.

Implication. Time, not inventory, is the leverage here. With the typical seller waiting six weeks for an offer and 17 listings already past 90 days, the buyer's position is stronger than the contract count implies — and the 90-day names are where a cut is most likely to be entertained. The Newport Heights $1.28M–$1.40M band remains the only place a 9/10 catchment is reachable under $1.5M. Breakeven stays highly sensitive to the appreciation assumption: at $1,500,000 it lands around year 14 at 3%/yr, slips to about year 27 at 1%, and never arrives inside 30 years at 0% — and with both ZIP medians negative YoY, the default 3% is an assumption, not an observation.

read.headline: 71 active listings, but only 18 of them sit in a 9/10 catchment — and at 6.66% the math still favours renting until roughly year 15.
points: Inventory is wide but shallow where it counts. Of 71 active 4BD homes under $2M, just 18 are zoned to one of the four target elementaries: Newport Heights 10, Somerset 6, Audubon 1, Woodridge 1. The other 53 come from the broad Redmond 98052 and Bellevue 98008 sweeps, where the elementary assignment still has to be confirmed address by address. Newport Heights is the only strong-school catchment offering real choice under $1.5M — five of its ten listings qualify, starting at $1,280,000. Somerset's six all open at $1,750,000 or above, and Audubon remains a one-home market.

Sellers are still the ones moving. The Aug 1 refresh logged 8 new listings against 5 price cuts totalling $292,500 and 6 homes leaving the market. Both core ZIP medians are negative year-over-year — Redmond 98052 at $1,302,113 (−3.9%) and Bellevue 98008 at $1,469,064 (−5.2%) — so the softness is showing up in the comparables, not just in individual negotiations. 29 of the 71 listings are now under $1.5M.

Financing is the headwind. The 30-yr fixed rose to 6.66% (Freddie Mac, Jul 30) from 6.58% the week before. On a $1.5M purchase at 20% down that is about $10,174/mo to own — $7,712 of it mortgage principal and interest, the rest tax, insurance and maintenance — against $4,772/mo for a comparable 4BD rental. Over a 7-year horizon at 3% appreciation, renting comes out roughly $179,000 cheaper, and buying does not pull ahead until around year 15.

A cheaper entry moves the breakeven far more than the rate does. Run the same model on the least expensive strong-school listing ($1,280,000, Newport Heights) and the monthly cost to own falls to about $8,704, the 7-year gap narrows to roughly $89,000, and breakeven arrives near year 11 — four years sooner. Reference home C ($1,548,900, unchanged this refresh) goes the other way: more house and nearly an acre, but about $10,501/mo, a Lake Hills 5/10 zone, and a wider 7-year gap of roughly $200,000 for the same year-15 breakeven.

What this implies. At 6.66% a purchase only clears the rent comparison on a long stay, so the school catchment — not the cost math — is what would justify buying now. Only 6 of the 71 listings are both under $1.5M and inside a 9/10 zone, and five of those are Newport Heights. That narrow band, from $1,280,000 up, is where the shortest breakeven and the strongest school overlap.
